utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, case number IT-01-47-T, the Prosecutor versus Enver Hadzihasanovic and Amir Kubura.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. I'll ask the sole representative of the Prosecution for the appearances now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours, Counsel, and everyone in and around the courtroom. For the Prosecution, Daryl Mundis, and our case manager, Mr. Andres Vatter. I anticipate that Ms. Tecla Benjamin will join us later in the course of today's proceedings. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could we have the appearances for the Defence, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. RESIDOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. President. Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of General Enver Hadzihasanovic, Edina Residovic, counsel; Stephane Bourgon, co-counsel; and Mirna Milanovic, our legal assistant. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. On behalf of Mr. Kubura, Rodney Dixon, Fahrudin Ibrisimovic, and Nermin Mulalic, our legal assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. The Trial Chamber would like to greet everyone present in the courtroom today, Mr. Mundis, Defence counsel, the accused. In particular, I would like to greet the Prosecution's new assistant, Mr. Andres Vatter, who started working yesterday. We have a witness scheduled for today, but before I let Mr. Mundis take the floor, I would like to render the following decision concerning the witnesses. The Trial Chamber, with regard to the explanations presented by the Prosecution about not calling the 19 witnesses, and after having heard the Defence's position, grants the Prosecution's wish not to call these witnesses. Nevertheless, with regard to one witness, Mr. Vlado Adamovic, a former judge, the Trial Chamber would like to invite the Prosecution who wanted to call the witness on the 25th of May, 2004 to inform the Trial Chamber that given the fact that they have requested that a number of documents concerning courts be tendered into evidence - concerning military and civilian courts - the Trial Chamber would like to know if they would like to reconsider their decision not to call this witness. In this case, in such a case it would be possible to hear the witness in order to authenticate certain documents mentioned and in order to provide the Trial Chamber with all the necessary information relating to the contents of these documents. Mr. Mundis, that would mean that the Trial Chamber has taken note of the fact that you don't want to call these 19 witnesses. Nevertheless, we would like to draw your attention to this one witness, and we would like to know whether given the fact that there are a number of documents that ought to be authenticated, you would like to call this witness after all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Upon reflection and in light of comments made by the Trial Chamber both yesterday and today, the Prosecution would respectfully request that our decision with respect to Mr. Adamovic be reconsidered, and consequently we would be in a position to bring Mr. Adamovic prior to the closing of the Prosecution case. Clearly, he will not be on the schedule as of 25 May. We will endeavour to bring him here during the first ten days of June and of course we'll notify the Trial Chamber and the Defence as soon as we have a confirmed date for the appearance of Mr. Adamovic. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. The Trial Chamber has taken note of what you have said, and this witness might be appearing as soon as possible, perhaps in the first part of the month of June. We have a witness scheduled for today, but there appears to be a problem. We will therefore go into private session, Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are in open session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can I ask a technical question, Your Honour?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I understand also French. Is it possible for me to listen to your questions in French, because it sort of confuses me when I understand both languages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you understand both languages; you can also answer in French if you like, as you wish.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I will answer in English, but I will listen the your language in French, the original. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that case, as far as the technicalities are concerned, it's sufficient for you to switch the microphone off if you don't want to hear what is being said. Please stand up, and you will read the solemn declaration out in English.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You may sit down now.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please approach the microphones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As I said, you will now have to answer the questions that will be put to you by the Prosecution, by Mr. Mundis, who is to your right. But before he takes the floor, I would like to provide you with other information. The procedure followed here has been adopted from the common-law system. Once the Prosecution has concluded its examination, Defence counsel will conduct their cross-examination, Defence counsel for the accused, who are at the back of the courtroom, and the Defence counsel is in front of them. They will ask you some questions, and you will see that the questions they put to you won't be identical or of the same kind as those of the Prosecution. They will be asking you questions to verify the credibility of your answers and also to obtain information regarding the political and military context or regarding any other matters that might be of interest to the Defence. Once this stage has been completed, the Prosecution may re-examine you. The three Judges sitting before you may at any stage in the proceedings ask you questions if they think that this might be useful, either because they want additional clarifications or because they believe that certain matters are not quite clear, and in order to establish the truth it's necessary to obtain additional information. In such cases, the Judges will ask you the questions they think are relevant. The Judges may ask you questions at any time, but as a general rule they prefer to wait for the examination-in-chief and cross-examination to be completed. After the Judges have asked you questions, the Prosecution and Defence counsel can also ask you additional questions. To the extent that this is possible, try to provide clear and precise answers to the questions. Since you understand a number of languages, this will be useful to everyone. If you feel that a question is too complicated, ask the person putting it to you to rephrase it in clear terms, because as the procedure here is basically an oral procedure, what you say is of crucial importance because we have nothing in writing concerning your testimony. So it is what is said that has importance. In addition, given that you have made a solemn declaration, false testimony should not be given. There is also another provision in the Rules. I will just remind you of it, but it is not something that should be applicable to you. A witness may always refuse to answer a question if the witness believes that his answer could be used against him at a subsequent date. In such a case, it is possible for the Trial Chamber to compel the witness to answer the question but the witness is granted a form of immunity. So this is, generally speaking, the procedure that will be followed in this courtroom. It might be very different from the procedure followed in your country. Having said that, I will give the floor to Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. Can you begin by telling the Trial Chamber a little bit about the United Nations Center for Human Rights and how that fits into the overall United Nations human-rights system.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: The UN Center for Human Rights, or UNCHR for short, it's a body which doesn't exist any more, which has evolved into the office of the high commissioner for human rights. But at that time it was the department, if you want, of United Nations Secretariat responsible for facilitating all sorts of human-rights-related mandate of the Secretary-General and of other United Nations bodies. In 1993, the UN Center for Human Rights, as mandated by the United Nations Commission for Human Rights, launched its first ever field operation in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, when did you begin working for the UN Center for Human Rights?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: In early 1993 I had been headhunted to be a part of this field operation. I think it was in February, February or March.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Witness, prior to joining the UN Center for Human Rights, where had you been employed and what was your background? In other words, why were you headhunted, as you put it, for this position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Immediately before joining the UN Center for Human Rights, I was a director of the Geneva-based small non-governmental association which dealt with human rights in Russia. That was for about two and a half years. Before that, I worked as an attache of the Russian - at the time Soviet - permanent mission in Geneva and my work line related also to human rights activities of the United Nations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell the Chamber what type of training or briefing you received prior to going to work for UN Center for Human Rights as it related to the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: I cannot recall of proper briefings or trainings. Me and my colleagues who were also employed as part of this operation, we just went through all kinds of reports and tried to familiarise ourselves as much as we could with the human rights and the political and military situation in the former Yugoslavia at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When did you first go to the former Yugoslavia in your capacity as a field officer and where were you based?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: I think it was May 1993, and the -- our logistical location was with the UNPROFOR HQ in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Besides yourself, Witness, how many other human-rights field officers worked for the UN center?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Initially there were two prior to my and my colleague's arrival. Then -- so basically there were four of us. And this figure fluctuated between three, four, and five; people came, people go. So it was the core personnel was about four or five strong at any given moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How long did you remain working for the UN Center for Human Rights in the former Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: In the former Yugoslavia itself, I worked for several months, almost a year. I left it in March 1994. Then I stayed for a couple of more months in the UN center in Geneva itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what your specific responsibilities were following your arrival in Zagreb in May of 1993.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: My responsibilities have changed. The initial idea was that I might proceed to Belgrade, but this didn't happen. Then I was assigned with the mandate to monitor human-rights situation in what was at that time called the United Nations Protected Areas or UNPAs, and in several weeks from then, certainly during the summer of 1993, I have been assigned with the human rights with Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How many other field officers worked in Bosnia for the UN center?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: At that time, it was my colleague and myself, before he left.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber, please, a little bit about how you actually functioned. What did you do? How did you go about doing it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Our mandate was to facilitate the activities of the United Nations Special Rapporteur, Tadeusz Mazowiecki, in supplying him with information, with evidence, with all sorts of rough or more sophisticated data about the human-rights situation in the former Yugoslavia. We have received allegations of all kinds of human rights violations and we tried to investigate in order to supply the Special Rapporteur with confirmed information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You've mentioned the Special Rapporteur. Can you please tell us a little bit about the relationship between the UN center field officers, human-rights field officers such as yourself, and the Special Rapporteur. What was the relationship?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: There was no direct relationship, apart, of course, the times when he himself went with the mission to the region. Otherwise, we have submitted our information via the UN Center for Human Rights in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit about the submitting of information. How did you do that? How frequently did you do that? What technical means did you use to submit information? These types of issues.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: The easiest part is that we have submitted it almost always by fax to Geneva. We don't know how -- I don't know how this information has been routed after that. In case of immediate urgency, we used to call him or establish conference calls with him. Periodically, it was dictated by the developments in the field, but I think that was what concern my area of responsibility, Bosnia. Geneva have counted on two to three reports per week, one of them sometimes brief, sometimes more extensive ones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe for us how you actually -- you told us that you received allegations and tried to confirm information contained in them. Can you tell us how you went about doing that.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Sometimes we saw this information -- sometimes information arrived to us via monitoring of the press or people called us or we read about this -- about certain things in UNPROFOR regular situation reports or special reports. Sometimes we saw this information actively by participating in all kinds of meetings, which were quite frequent during that time, inter-agency meetings in Zagreb. And we spoke to journalists, who were sometimes willing to reveal more than what you could read in the press. So our -- we didn't exclude no possibility. We didn't ignore any information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How did you go about investigating the information that you received from these different sources? What did you actually do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Speaking about Bosnia, the best means to investigate was to organise the field trip. If the allegation was not that serious or we have some doubts about its authenticity, sometimes it was enough just to call several other sources and to cross-reference it. And so at a certain threshold we made a decision whether an allegation deserves a field trip or it does not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: From your arrival and assuming responsibilities for Bosnia until the end of 1993, approximately how many such field trips did you make to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: I cannot recall the exact amount, because some of these trips were really short ones, for a day -- it was a matter of a day or two. I think -- major ones I remember, I hope, quite well. There were probably three or four of them. By "major" I mean taking five -- from five to ten days. Also, I would include accompanying the Special Rapporteur himself, although it was a short trip; also the media, I think. I think I've been there on a regular basis at least once a month.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How did you actually conduct these field trips, again from a technical point of view? Who went with you? Where did you access vehicles and support and logistics? How did that work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: I preferred to go alone, because Bosnia was a dangerous place and I was the only one responsible for Bosnia, so to the extent possible I discouraged my colleagues to go with me. But of course in the field I was not alone. I was accompanied either by military -- sometimes protected by the military or by civil affairs officers of UNPROFOR. And before going, all the details had to be processed and agreed and discussed, either with civilian affairs officers or with the military component of UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Throughout this period from mid-1993 through the end of 1993, when you were the field officer for Bosnia, where were you actually living? I understand that's a difficult term, but where were you actually based?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: The logistical base was in UNPROFOR HQ in Zagreb. I rented an apartment not far from the office. An office was just a tiny container. So I spent my free time in Zagreb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, you've mentioned the logistical support that you received from the civilian affairs officers or the military component of UNPROFOR. Can you tell us a little bit about that structure in Bosnia and how you were able to liaise with them and coordinate your efforts with them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: It took me some time to understand how UNPROFOR worked and how its military and civilian components coordinated their activities with each other. Basically, we would inform about our problems or about our plans the civilian affairs on the highest possible level. We would get their agreement in principle, a promise of support, and then went down the administrative ladder to contact civil-affairs officers in concrete localities. It was basically the same with the military component. Every time we went, we received adequate support but it had to be cleared previously with those in military authority, in Zagreb and in locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where was the UNPROFOR headquarters that you dealt with in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Several ones. Of course, it was obvious to contact military personnel in Sarajevo when we have arrived. One of the major logistical bases was in Kiseljak, BH command, and since a lot of what I had to do was around Central Bosnia, the HQ of the British Battalion Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, you've mentioned BH command in Kiseljak. Can you tell the Trial Chamber a little bit about what that was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: It was a big hotel, a spa, full with international and military personnel from all countries, a very busy place, helicopters landing and lifting every half an hour. It was used as a major logistical point of -- to conduct military -- not military but UNPROFOR mandate to perform mandate in all the territory of Bosnia, from Tuzla down to Mostar.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Just to clarify. When we talk about BH command in Kiseljak, that was UNPROFOR; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us earlier about the field trips that you took into Bosnia from your base in Zagreb. Can you tell us about the first such trip that you made, approximately when that was and what the purpose of that trip was and where you went.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: It was in early June 1993. The purpose of that trip was basically to get myself more familiar with the area and with the people. I was taken on that trip by my colleague, who was responsible for Bosnia but who was supposed to leave the field operation, and it was what military could qualify as a reconnaissance trip. It was supposed to be so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And where exactly did you go on that trip, if you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Our destination was British Battalion in Vitez. And we went there through Sarajevo and Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall any of the people that you may have met on that first trip, particularly when you went to Vitez? Any of the local, political, or military leaders?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: At that time, we did not establish -- try to establish any contact with the local, political, or military leaders. Of course, I remember - and this is an unforgettable experience - the visit to the British Battalion. And we also met other people, but I cannot qualify them as political or military leaders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: While you were on this first trip, did you at any time meet with anyone who raised any type of allegations of human-rights violations with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Yes. The next day of our arrival in Vitez, we were informed by I think an officer on duty that there was someone at the gate of the base with a story about a human-rights violation and a massacre was referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you in fact meet with the individual who was at the gate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Yes. We made on on-the-spot decision to talk to this person.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of this individual?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: I remember the initials, I think BMM, but I don't think I'd remember the exact name. It was Berislav or Borislav, the first name, and I can't remember the second name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall any of the specifics about what this person told you, in terms of the location of the alleged crimes and what exactly happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: I remember quite well. It was my first encounter of this type, my first interview with an allegation of a major violation of humanitarian law. So I remember it quite well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please tell us what you recall from meeting with this individual, what he told you about, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: He told us we were - the two of us - to conduct this interview, and at that time my linguistic skills didn't -- were just rudimentary. So my colleague had to translate some -- a lot of it, but not all. He told us that several days ago he was a member of a group of civilians and prisoners of war which had been summarily executed not far from the place called Maljine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall any of the specifics as to what this individual told you about who may have committed this offence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: He referred that after some fighting a group of people were collected by members of the attacking Muslim forces. He was a part of Croats, some of them military, some not, some wounded, some not. And he continuously referred to Muslim soldiers as being the ones who did that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bourgon, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. Your Honours, I would like to draw your attention to the fact that the person that the witness met is the person who has already testified before this Trial Chamber. Since this is hearsay evidence, there's no need for my learned friend to ask these questions, because we already had the information from the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But the witness can tell us that he met this person because for the time being we only have the name -- the first name of that person and not the last name. You may continue, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, the individual that you met with, did that person provide you with any information that would be of assistance in terms of conducting an investigation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Do you mean our investigation at that time or the current proceedings?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your investigation at that time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Yes. At our request, he drew a small map of the place and marked an exact location when this incident occurred.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you recall any of the other information that this witness provided to you at the time concerning himself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Yes. He showed us the wounds -- not the wound itself, but one small -- I don't know the word in English. The wound had been treated. He did not provide a lot of background on himself personally, but he insisted continuously that he was not a part of the military, that he was not among those who participated in the fighting at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, what if anything did you do with the information that this individual provided to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: We took our notes with us to Zagreb. We typed in a report in a matter of days and submitted this report to Geneva. And kept all the originals, our notes, and the map with our files in the office.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At any subsequent time did you take up some kind of follow-up action with respect to this allegation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Yes. This has been, as I've told you, my first encounter with such circumstances, and the village of Maljine has remained a professional challenge to me. So I kept making inquiries wherever I could about any possible additional details. I was quite consistent in trying to establish the truth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you recall any of the individuals to whom you made such inquiries and when, approximately?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: I think every time I went to Central Bosnia I made these inquiries with the relevant civilian or military personnel of UNPROFOR. I made these inquiries with local, political, or military commanders, personnel. We discussed this case with colleagues both in the office and from other agencies working in the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Following this first field mission in June of 1993 where you were in Vitez, when was the next time you were in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: I could have made a couple of short trips, the details of which I don't remember, apart from some major details. During one of these short trips, it was possible for us to meet with Dr. Karadzic, but that was a short trip. My next extensive trip was to the area was in late September 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where did you go in late September 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: This was a complicated trip. I've covered -- I've been to several locations during seven or eight days I've been on the field. I think my itinerary was Sarajevo; Kiseljak; of course; Zenica; Vitez; Busovaca; Travnik, including the village of Maljine; Bugojno; Gornji Vakuf; Tomislavgrad; and then back to Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you have any -- you told us earlier that you'd had meetings with political and military commanders. Did you have any such meetings in Zenica in late September 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: It's correct we've had meeting with the mayor of Zenica, I can't -- or was it deputy mayor, and with the deputy commander of the 3rd Corps of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the name of the deputy commander of the 3rd Corps of the BH army that you met?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Very well. He was introduced to us as Merdan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what issues you discussed with Merdan in late September 1993.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: A lot of issues about humanitarian or military aspects which might have influenced human-rights situation, and also some issues regarding the ways the BH army conducted its war operations. We have also discussed a little bit the issue of this allegation of mass execution in Maljine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you elaborate for us a little bit about, when you say, "some issues regarding the ways the BH army conducted its war operations." What do you mean by that and what do you recall specifically talking about?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: At his own initiative, Mr. Merdan provided an expose about his and his superior's efforts to build a disciplined army. It was also in the relation to this issue and to my request to get access to Maljine that he declined to do so, saying that BH army is a disciplined army and the soldiers follow orders and they don't -- there is no need for him to provide any additional written permissions. So that was more or less the discussion about the ways of BH army at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I'd like to focus again a little bit on Maljine. Do you recall the efforts you took with Merdan to go to Maljine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Yes. I mentioned Maljine several times. I indicated my itinerary to him, and I shared the information I had, in a sort of sketch about the allegations in Maljine, and I requested permission from him facilitating my possible visit to this village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall if Merdan responded to you in any way when you raised the allegations about Maljine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: I do. He told me and those who accompanied me that he's aware of the allegations, but nothing of this sort took place; that even if there were some mass graves in the area, this would be the graves where the soldiers killed in action were buried. So he totally denied even this possibility of such an occurrence to take place.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What steps did you take to gain access to Maljine, in terms of discussions with Mr. Merdan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: There were not much steps to be taken. I understood that this discussion was leading nowhere. So during that conversation, I dropped the subject, but I contradicted him about the extent to the discipline in the BH army at that time and I indicated to him cases when a written permission from him had in fact been required by the soldiers at the checkpoints.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did Mr. Merdan give you any written permission to pass through the checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Negative. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, for clarification, why not?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: The reason for his refusal to do so, as I've said, was his conviction that the chain of command in BH army has been established, that his subordinates follow the orders, and the order in this case would be for the local commander to take a decision taking first into consideration the reasons related to my safety.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Other than Maljine and these discussions on the professionalism in the Army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, what else did you discuss with Merdan?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: We've mentioned the issue of Guca Gora, which was another -- which is a location not far from Maljine, and all sorts of general issues. This was not a very lengthy conversation, I think. It didn't last more than an hour, hour and a half. A big part of it was consumed by his initial statements about the BH army, and then you also have to consider the translation. So really there was not much time for any detailed conversations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What, if anything, did Mr. Merdan tell you about foreign fighters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: This issue has in fact been mentioned. I asked this question. He did not deny the presence of foreign fighters, or at that time they were called Mujahedin, but I referred to them as volunteers who came to fight and who are fighting in his army in -- and who follow orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall having any discussions with Mr. Merdan concerning the civilian population in the area controlled by the 3rd Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Yes. But I was not too attentive to that, because just before that I had the meeting with the mayor of Zenica, and at that time a very detailed briefing on the situation of the civilian population had been provided to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Following this meeting with Mr. Merdan in late September 1993, where did you go next or where did your investigation concerning Maljine take you next?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Concerning Maljine, it was in Travnik, Stari Vitez, and Maljine itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit about how it came to be that you were able to go to Maljine.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: In Travnik, bypassing Vitez, we got acquainted with the deputy mayor of Travnik and with Salko Beba, who was at that time deputy head of the -- or maybe head of the exchange commission. There were mentioned the issue of Maljine, and I think I convinced Mr. Beba to try and escort me up to Maljine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall any of the specifics of your conversation with Mr. Beba about access to Maljine, what he told you, what you asked him, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: I asked him whether it would be possible to get there, because from Travnik it was really very -- a very short drive. I told him about my conversation with Merdan and about Mr. Merdan's reluctance to issue a written permission. I think this annoyed Mr. Beba quite a lot because he was of the opinion that without such a written permission this would have been impossible. We also had discussed the issues of the participation of foreign fighters, or Mujahedin, in the BH army, and we had discussed other incidents which have allegedly occurred during the June 1993 offensive of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What if anything do you recall Mr. Beba telling you about foreign fighters or Mujahedin in the BH army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: We had a conversation on this subject, and I think he told me that this role of Mujahedin has evolved once they were - some of them were really, came there to fight; others increasingly took an ideological and indoctrination role, education role, and private soldiers with ideological influence. But others, some were active fighters. And my impression was that he was of the opinion that not all of those who fought really fulfilled the orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you on this day in September 1993 go anywhere with Mr. Salko Beba?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Yes. After that meeting in Travnik, we went together to Guca Gora and to Maljine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what you saw in Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: In Guca Gora there was a big church or even a monastery. There was not much to be seen the allegation of -- to the fact that there was a detention centre did not prove correct. I did not find any evidence to that. It was more or less well maintained, although there were evidence of recent fighting and some desecration of religious objects. There were some soldiers who looked like they were protecting the property in Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: While you were in Guca Gora, did you see anyone else that might be described as a soldier?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: As a soldier, maybe not; but as a fighting element, definitely yes. I got a glimpse of a car which was transporting Mujahedin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber about what you observed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: We were standing and talking outside of the monastery when a car full of people, some of them inside, some of them outside of the car, some armed, some not, sped by us. These people were wearing -- some of them were wearing white fatigues, so they didn't look like normal elements of the BH army. They were carrying some slogans and banners with Arabic inscriptions on them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you discuss what you had seen with Mr. Beba?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: There was not much to discuss. It was obvious to both of us that these were foreign fighters, and the physical reaction of Mr. Beba indicate to me that he would be unwilling to discuss this. He was obviously displeased with this view.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us where you went after leaving Guca Gora.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: After leaving Guca Gora and securing permission of the local commander which was located there, we proceeded to Maljine.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately what time on this day in September 1993 you arrived in Maljine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: It had been four or five hours in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So between 4.00 and 5.00 in the afternoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: About 4.00 and 5.00 hours. It was a couple of hours after we finished lunch, so -- but it was still daylight, so it couldn't have been later than 5.00 or 4.30 in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what you did upon arrival in Maljine on that afternoon.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: After we left Guca Gora, Mr. Beba stopped showing the way, but I tried to remember as well as I could the map and the drawing of -- which had been provided to me in June. So we've made our way both to village of Maljine and to a small hamlet of Bikosi, which was just above and which had been indicated to us as the site of the mass killing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were there other people present in Maljine when you arrived there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Yes. There were four, maybe five males of fighting age. I didn't see that they were armed, but they were in camouflage and they were basically hanging around.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What, if anything, did you say to any of these people that you found when you arrived in Maljine?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Not much. When I arrived in Maljine and discovered that wall, I just stood there silently for several minutes and nobody asked me any question. I didn't ask any question at that time. It was just after some time that I asked them about the nature of the pile of fresh earth which was right behind that wall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What, if anything, did you say about this pile of fresh earth behind the wall?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Since I had doubts that this would be the mass grave - I had an earlier indication that the mass grave is located elsewhere - I didn't press them so hard. I just asked them what's the reason for this, for this pile of earth. And the answer was that they didn't know. It was earth which has been turned years ago. This pile was made years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, when you said that, you smiled and chuckled a little bit. Why did you have that reaction?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: It was an obvious lie because it -- nothing was growing on this pile of earth. So it was obvious to me that it's -- that it's several days, weeks maximum.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you make any additional inquiries about this pile of fresh earth to the local people that you encountered?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: No. I think at a certain stage during this very brief conversation it became clear that my reasons for being there were clear. And the frustration of one of - I can't call them soldiers, one of the local people - with my -- what they could have interpreted as joy was such that he volunteered to bring a shovel so that I start digging for bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So he actually offered to give you a shovel so that you could begin digging.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Approximately how long did you -- let me ask you: Did you in fact conduct any type of digging or exhumation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How long did you remain in Maljine on that afternoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Maybe half an hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where did you go after that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: After that, if I'm not mistaken, we went further south to Bugojno.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: When you say "we," who was with you at this point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Up to the checkpoints, we've been escorted by Salko Beba and a couple of his colleagues. Then we proceeded together with the civil affairs, who accompanied me during this trip, civil affairs from Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, after this period in September 1993, did you have any additional discussions concerning Maljine with political or military leaders in Central Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Not that I can recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What steps did you take to record the information that you received based on the mission?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: As usual, after my report -- after this trip, I made a report, and this was very -- quite an extensive report, at least 15 pages. There were other findings -- findings to report upon -- to report on. Maljine took just -- it was just a section. And this report has been submitted to Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: To your knowledge, Witness, were any reports or letters based on the information that you produced drafted to anyone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Yes. As a part of this report in its concluding part, I suggest that the Special Rapporteur write to the Bosnian Presidency and call his attention and the attention of other authority in Bosnia-Herzegovina to the allegations, sometimes quite credible allegations, about mass killings which have been attributed to the Muslim army.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I would ask that the witness be shown Prosecution Exhibit 170.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, I'd ask you to take a look at Prosecution Exhibit 170, and particularly the second and third page of that document. Have you seen this document before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Yes, I have seen that document before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit about this document, what it is and when you might have seen it.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: This is a letter from the Special Rapporteur, Mr. Tadeusz Mazowiecki, to the president of the Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Mr. Izetbegovic, calling the attention of the president to the allegations of atrocities committed in Central Bosnia. I can see that Maljine is mentioned in this letter, as well as other allegations, so I would assume that this letter -- the decision about sending this letter -- my proposal might have been instrumental in appearance of this letter.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you've also mentioned that you sent faxes as part of your reporting data.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask that the witness now be shown Prosecution Exhibit 277.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Yes, I am.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber what this document is.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: This is a translation from the article which had been published in one of major Croatian newspapers at that time, Vjesnik, and that was an article about an allegation of mistreatment of Croats in the regions under Muslim control in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Who sent this information up to the UN Center for Human Rights?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: At my request, this article had been translated by our local translators, and I have just sent it to bring the attention of my superiors in Geneva to this irresponsible journalism, and I say "irresponsible," as we'd been able to verify the -- some of the facts stated here did not in fact happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, I have just a few final questions for you. The discussions that you had or any of your time at BH command in Kiseljak, did you ever discuss with anyone in UNPROFOR foreign fighters in the 3rd Corps area of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Yes. We've -- that was the way we operated. We discussed everything what was on our minds with colleagues and the issue of Mujahedin had continuously been mentioned in my discussions with journalists, with military personnel, both of UNPROFOR and the ECMM.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you remember if anyone at BH command in Kiseljak gave you any documents relating to foreign fighters or Mujahedin?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: I do. A document had been given to me, but it was not really in the context of any discussion on Mujahedin; just my attention had been drawn to a translation of kind of an instruction for Muslim soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you remember who gave you this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You mentioned that it was a translation. Do you remember seeing an original-language version of this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: These were just several sheets of papers stapled together. The first page was in Serbo-Croatian language, and then there was several pages of English text.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: With the assistance of the usher, I would ask that the witness be shown the document P11, which is marked for identification.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, I would ask you to briefly look through this document. And you've told us that you saw certain parts of the translation of this document. I would like you to see if you see the portions that you were provided by BH command.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: I would recall now that the names of the authors also were on the page in Serbo-Croatian which I received in the BH command. The date also fits, and on the second page, this -- the initial inscription in -- I suppose in Arabic was the same. Otherwise, the printing is very different. These are not the fonts which were used in BH command or also UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you see -- if you could briefly thumb through this document, do you see those portions of this translated version that you were provided with by BH command in Kiseljak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Do I have time to go through this?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I also note the time. I know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Take your time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, sir. I've found something in this document which I was in those pages which were given to me, which you referred to.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you please tell us in the English translation, P11, marked for identification, what page or pages you were provided with by BH command in Kiseljak.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: I'm not 100 per cent sure because it was a long time ago since I was provided those pages. But I remember seeing in those pages texts, paragraphs which referred to prisoners of war and to suicide.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, can you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: These are pages 24 and 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: With respect to the information that you were shown at BH command in Kiseljak relating to prisoners of war, what was your reaction upon reading that information from this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: I can't remember having any particular reaction, since the status of these documents were not clear to me. I didn't -- it didn't look like a book of orders or a code for BH army. It looked more like a religious text, so there was nothing which I was concerned about in terms of my work. But I remember there was a piece about a possibility to kill prisoners of war if the commander decides so. And this got my attention. But again, I didn't know the status of this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber why that particular provision caught your attention at that time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Because of many allegations, including Maljine, which for me has ceased to be an allegation. There were reports about murder of prisoners of war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, I note the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's 10.30. We'll have a 25-minute break, and we will resume at about 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, you may proceed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. The Prosecution has completed its direct examination of the witness. I would ask that Prosecution Exhibit P11 be returned from the witness to the registrar. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Mundis, are you trying to tell us that you wanted this document to be admitted into evidence? Do you want this document to be admitted into evidence? Because for the time being, it was just marked for identification. Do you want to have this document admitted?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Not at this time, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well, then. I'm going to give the floor to the Defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Mr. President, I would like to go into private session for the beginning of my cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, can we go into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, we are back in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: [In English] Witness ZO, you were at that time offered this three-months temporary contract, which was, as you mentioned to me yesterday, according with the United Nations employment system, at the professional level 3.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: This is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Or P3, as we --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: -- commonly know. You were a field officer, human rights, and this was the first time that the United Nations deployed such a mission for a conflict area; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: This is also correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the period you were attached to the Center for Human Rights during that time was from March of 1993 until June of 1994. Now, that is with the centre itself.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But the time you were working specifically for the mission in the former Yugoslavia - that is, in Zagreb - was from May of 1993 to March of 1994, which includes a period of ten months.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: This is correct. I'm sure your calculation is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And you mentioned to me yesterday that you did four or five major missions during that time, which were about five days or more.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And that you also completed five to six short missions of one or two days.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: I would assume it is correct. To the best of my recollection, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And that in any event you tried to go out to the field at least once a month.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And you mentioned that there were four to five of you in Zagreb and that this is where you were stationed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And that in Zagreb you, to use common language, did not have a boss.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: This is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Your immediate supervisor was the chief of the Special Procedures Section in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the Special Procedures Section is the office in Geneva which facilitates the work of the Special Rapporteur.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Facilitated at that time. I don't know the structure of the Office of the High Commissioner right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And in your case, your work and your mandate was related to the work of the Special Rapporteur on human rights for the former Yugoslavia, and that was Mr. Tadeusz Mazowiecki.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Very much so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the Office of the Special Rapporteur was actually not in Zagreb or in Geneva but somewhere in Poland, and you may have mentioned Warsaw yesterday.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Its physical location was somewhere in Poland. I would assume this would be Warsaw.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, the way the information went from your work up to the Special Rapporteur was information taken from the field, taken to Zagreb; somehow analysed in Zagreb, forwarded to Geneva to the Special Procedures Section; somehow packaged and sent to the Special Rapporteur; is that a fair illustration of the process?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: This is a fair illustration, apart from extreme urgencies when we established conferences call with the Special Rapporteur directly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And sometimes you had requests to look into specific events, whereas on other occasions you set your own agenda.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And if you happened to write a report for the benefit of the Special Rapporteur, it would not be uncommon for a two-page report to be brought down to approximately two lines in the report of the Special Rapporteur; but sometimes it could be the other way around.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Geneva was the place where they -- the term you used yesterday "packaged" your reports into information that could be of use to the Special Rapporteur.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that the Special Rapporteur himself had a clear mandate which is defined in a Security Council resolution, and that is to observe and report on the human rights situation and, if so, on human-rights violations in the former Yugoslavia; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Again, partially. Initially this was the resolution by the UN commission on human rights, which was only indirectly approved by the Security Council.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But his mandate was quite clear, in terms of what he was to focus on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And you also mentioned in a statement you provided to the Office of the Prosecution that you thought that your mandate, your personal mandate, was somewhat less clear, although it was derived from the mandate of the Special Rapporteur.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And you also mentioned that the work of field officers was sometimes driven by events; whereas you would show up in the field, something would take place, and that could modify your agenda.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And you also mentioned, Witness ZO, that the sources for determining whether a field mission was necessary included the press; conversations with journalists; reports from ECMM, including special reports, as well as reports from the civil affairs officers; and even sometimes from UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Is that quite a thorough list of the sources you consulted to make up your mind on whether a field mission would be necessary?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, on this basis, you proposed your own field missions which were then approved by Geneva, unless, of course, there was a specific requirement by the Special Rapporteur.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So you were kind of in a relative freedom with minimum guidance.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, before looking at the two visits that were discussed this morning by my colleague from the Prosecution, I would just like to confirm that when you took this job you had, of course, a background in human rights, but would it be fair to say that you had no experience in terms of conducting investigations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: This would be correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And that at that time you had never been to Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And that, as you mentioned yesterday, you knew very little about the conflict that was going on in Bosnia and Herzegovina or on the intention or the legal status of the warring parties.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: I didn't know much more than had been reported in the press and other media.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And would it be fair to say - and I take this from our discussion yesterday - that in order for someone to understand what is going on in Bosnia at that time, it would take a good three to four months for one person focussing on the military, political, or in terms of the involvement of the international community? Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: That would be fair.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, your aim in conducting field missions was not to investigate as we understand the word "investigate," but it was more like fact-finding to determine if human-rights violations had been committed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In this respect, your objective was not to determine who had committed a particular violation but to gather sufficient information for the benefit of the Special Rapporteur.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Sometimes this information would include indications of who would be the alleged perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But of course that was not the aim, the purpose of your missions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: [No audible response]

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, if we move to your first mission in June in Central Bosnia. Can you confirm, Witness ZO, that this was in fact your first field mission and your first time ever in Bosnia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: I would confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And that your aim going on this mission was to accompany another field officer whose term was ending, namely, Mr. Thomas Osorio; and it was also to know people and to provide you with some experience in the field, because this was a first.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness ZO, I must bring you back to a question where your response was not recorded on the transcript, and I refer you to -- my question was: But of course that was not the aim or the purpose of your missions. And I was referring then to identify the identity of a perpetrator. Can you state your answer once again.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: That was not the aim of our mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness ZO. I move on to Thomas Osorio, who had developed very good contacts with the British Battalion in Vitez and, namely with three individuals, Colonel Stewart, who was the commander of BritBat; Randy Rhodes, who was the civil-affairs officer; and Mr. Steven Wolfson, who was from the UNHCR.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: I think I met Steven Wolfson after that June trip, and I doubt very much this they are acquainted, Thomas and Steven Wolfson. Otherwise, the first two individuals you mentioned were introduced to me by Thomas Osorio.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So he had got contacts with the first two, namely Colonel Stewart and Randy Rhodes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: And he had much more extensive contacts, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Witness ZO. Now, correct me if I'm wrong, but you mentioned that there was no official link between your work and the United Nations Commission of Experts which was conducting field investigation at the same time with the assistance of many states.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: There was no such link.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall if the findings that you made were ever communicated to the United Nations Commission of Experts?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: I would assume that would be a natural thing to be done by our superiors and colleagues in Geneva.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And can you confirm, Witness ZO, whether as a whole, if we look at the individuals who were part of your office - I refer to one name, Mr. Payam Akhavan, for example - that as a whole when the people of your section were recruited, they were not recruited on the basis of experience in the field of investigations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: I don't understand the link with Payam here. Can you rephrase or please be more specific in your question, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness ZO. I will try to be more precise. You mentioned a little earlier that you yourself did not have a background in terms of conducting investigations. If you can say, can we say -- draw the same conclusion from the other members of your section, in general?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: I think we have been headhunted for different reasons. All of us had our strengths and our weaknesses. I've indicated mine. I don't know and wouldn't like to interpret what were the considerations for hiring and assigning tasks to my other colleagues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That's very wise and respectable of you, --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: -- Witness ZO. If I may move to that trip in Bosnia, that is it took place in the first week of June. Did it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And your itinerary at that time was from -- first from Sarajevo to Vitez and you were transported by a Danish armoured personnel carrier; and from -- sorry, to Kiseljak and from Kiseljak to Vitez you were transported by a British Warrior with BritBat and you arrived there late at night.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And that night you mentioned that you went to the mess, that is, the officers' mess, and that you met with those who had access to those premises within the British Battalion.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, I understand, Witness ZO, or I'm not -- I don't know if you have a military background, but can you confirm that the mess or the officers' mess, from what you saw or from what you know, was kind of a social club for officers where people have a drink and exchange their war stories for the day in a relaxed atmosphere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: You're right about me not having a military background. You are also right about my impression of what the officers mess at the British Battalion was at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, before you went on this mission, Witness ZO, you mentioned that you had some information on a potential human rights violations in Guca Gora and Maljine; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: It is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And you also mentioned that you had no other information on any other potential human-rights violations which could have been committed in other towns.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: I don't remember, maybe because Maljine and Guca Gora were these two locations which kept being discussed in the days which followed this -- the planning of this trip.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, you knew about the massacre in Ahmici, but correct me if I'm wrong, but you were not aware of events such as what took place in Bandol or in Velika Bukovica, for example.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: The names of these locations don't seem -- don't sound familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And if in the reports which were accessible to you in Zagreb some events were mentioned of other violations, then it would have been your decision to focus on Maljine and not on something else.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: I would like to repeat that the purpose of this first trip was just a reconnaissance, to get to know people, to get people to know me. This was not planned as a fact-finding mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness ZO. Now, when you met the BritBat personnel initially, there was limited time for them to brief you. And if I quote you correctly, Thomas Osorio did most of the talking and of the arrangements.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: I think that we've spent not more than one hour maximum. It may even be 40 minutes in the mess, and then some sleeping arrangements were made. Thomas might have stayed a little bit later, but I went to bed rather -- not early, but earlier than Thomas.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So more importantly, what BritBat -- or what you could obtain from the British Battalion was a feel for the military situation in order for you to know where you could and where you could not go. And this was done by both you and Thomas Osorio or just by Thomas Osorio?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: I think it didn't even went to that stage in the briefing when we would receive advice where we could go or where we couldn't go. It was maybe just a general assessment of recent and current military aspects of the picture in the field in Central Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned that initially the issue of violations of human rights was not discussed with personnel from BritBat.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Definitely not during that first evening.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, maybe it's a mistake or maybe it's a question of memory, but I would just like to refer to you, Witness ZO, to the report you prepared when you returned to Zagreb after your first trip. And this report basically states -- let me just find it. I have lots of paper here. I had almost everything ready, but my colleague caught me off surprise by closing his examination-in-chief five minutes too early. If I may just report to this statement that you -- or this report which you completed in Zagreb in which you mentioned that in Kiseljak you were actually given a communique by someone related to the leadership of Croatia and the leadership of Herceg-Bosna and which was also addressed to the HINA news agency about allegations of a mass execution and that this was given to you by the civil affairs officer. Do you recall this at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: I don't recall this at all, but I don't exclude that while we were at Kiseljak and, again, being introduced to people, I could have been given some materials.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And I just read from that background information which was provided to us, and it says here: "The allegation of a mass execution reached us at BH command HQ on 11 June. Civil affairs received by telex a communique." And it talks about leadership of Croatia and Herceg-Bosna, HVO command, and HINA news agency; and that the same night when you arrived at British Battalion, "it was explained to us that a man from Maljine now staying in Vitez with some connections to the local HDZ leadership delivered the text of the communique to the gate on Thursday, the 10th of June." Is that -- do you recall these events at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: I recall this being a part of mine and Thomas's report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the events themselves, you don't recall -- or could it be that it is Mr. Osorio who received these things or ...?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: It could have been. And the report I think was the report which was drafted together by two of us, so the two of us contributed to the drafting of this report, and I can't really remember how we shared the labour.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, the next day, Witness ZO, a man called Niko came to the gate and he wanted to see you, and he promised that he would return with two victims of this alleged event, and he actually came back an hour and a half later with the person which you actually proceeded to interview.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: At this stage, I doubt that this man called Niko wanted to see me or us, and Thomas, because I doubt that he would have any sort of information that we were in the compounds of the British Battalion. Maybe he wanted to see anybody from civil affairs and it happened that two human rights field officers were on the spot, a coincidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But you did have a conversation with a gentleman called Niko, who introduced you to the person you interviewed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: I don't recall being in any contact with anybody except that gentleman. Thomas might have been in contact with the man called Niko. I don't think that I was present. If it happened, I was not present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness ZO, I mean, I perfectly understand that these things took place ten years ago, but the report says that on June 12th "Niko at 10.00 at his own initiative came to the gate and we talked to him. He promised that he will return with both witnesses mentioned in the communique in order to be interviewed by us. He returned after 1.5 hours with one of the witnesses. The second witness was impossible to be found. And we interviewed him for one hour." Is that -- could things have developed in this way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: They could. When in this report you see "us" or "we" it would not necessarily mean that we were doing everything in -- at the same time. So my memory -- first, my memory might fail me, because it was 11 years ago; and second, an explanation might be that Thomas did the conversation. But since we both were signing for the report, it would be natural for us to refer to "us" as a team.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, this gentleman, Niko, do you remember him at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But you do remember the communique.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: The communique --

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Which was -- which came from the leadership of the HDZ and which talked about these allegations.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: I do remember some papers which were given to us in Kiseljak. I don't remember in which language they were. During this first day or two in the field, I really had to rely a lot on my more experienced colleague to sort through the things and to sort through our priorities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: But could you confirm, Witness ZO, that as a matter of fact this interview that you conducted that day was not a planned event, that it happened on the ground, and that it was triggered by this communique from someone affiliated to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Could you please repeat your question or rephrase it, because this would seem to be as interpretation of events for me and I would rather be reluctant to interpret something which I vaguely remember happened 11 years ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And I have no problems whatsoever in maybe breaking down the question. Would you agree that this interview was not a planned event?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And it happened as a result of the communique.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Of this I am not sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And if it did happen as a result of the communique, because you don't remember, you knew that this communique came from people affiliated to the leadership of the HDZ, the HVO command -- or the HVO command.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: At that time, I had certain difficulty in understanding the difference between "HVO" and "HDZ," so I was very fresh in the field. I don't exclude that this could have been a planned action, but nothing had at that time caught my attention that it could have been an artificially-staged incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness ZO. Now, during this interview, you mentioned that you took some notes but that it was difficult to get everything due to the language issue, because Thomas Osorio spoke Bosnian or B/C/S very well and there was no interpreters and you spoke Russian, English, French, but a little bit of B/C/S. Would that be a fair statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: I didn't speak B/C/S at all at that time. Some words I could understand. French and Russian was never employed during this interview or my subsequent interviews. Thomas did a lot of talking, translated some of his questions and some of the answers. Sometimes I would put a question which Thomas would translate, and translate the answer back to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Witness ZO, can you confirm that this was a difficult moment for you since it was the first time that you were interviewing a witness talking about some very bad events?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: I can confirm that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In any event, your report that I referred to was drafted in Zagreb and both you and Thomas Osorio did it together.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And the report is the sum of both of your observations.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS ZO
